content: {"id": "99ed90ac-c918-4411-b70a-92ed52f07010", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "A domain-joined Windows Server 2019 EC2 instance fails patching with 0x8024002E and Windows Update says 'Some settings are managed by your organization'. The registry shows NoAutoUpdate=1 under HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Policies\\Microsoft\\Windows\\WindowsUpdate\\AU. Can I just set it to 0?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "397c2f12-4ca3-4f5b-b6f4-66fee102dfea", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "Windows Update Group Policy Registry Modification Approach"}]}

{"id": "420ce208-85fc-4a05-8fb6-09c3fde8c778", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Short answer: you *can*, but on a domain-joined instance it probably won't stick — and if it does stick, it'll likely get overwritten again on the next Group Policy refresh (every 90–120 minutes by default).

Here's why: `NoAutoUpdate=1` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\AU` is a policy-managed key, not a plain configuration setting. On a domain-joined machine, that key is almost always being written by a GPO (either a dedicated Windows Update policy or something bundled into a baseline/security GPO) rather than set manually. That's exactly what triggers the "Some settings are managed by your organization" message you're seeing — Windows is telling you GPO owns that value.

If you edit the registry directly:
- It may get reverted at the next `gpupdate` cycle (background refresh or manual `gpupdate /force`)
- Even if it doesn't revert immediately, you're fighting the actual source instead of fixing it, so it'll likely recur on this instance or any other instance in the same OU
- The 0x8024002E error itself (WU being disabled/blocked by policy) should clear once the policy source is actually fixed, not just the registry symptom

The right fix is usually one of:
1. Find which GPO is applying this setting (`gpresult /h report.html` on the box, or check Group Policy Management for the OU this EC2 instance's computer object lives in) and either exclude this instance or change the policy
2. If patching is meant to be handled by SSM Patch Manager / WSUS instead of Windows Update directly, confirm that's the intended design — `NoAutoUpdate=1` is sometimes set deliberately so WSUS/SSM is the sole patching path, and the real question becomes "why isn't SSM patching succeeding," not "why is WU disabled"

Want me to look into which patching mechanism (WSUS, SSM Patch Manager, or direct WU) is actually configured for this instance, or pull the current GPO-applied WU settings to confirm the policy source?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
